name: Cyber-Physical & Autonomous Vehicle Security
description: Security of cyber-physical systems, ICS/SCADA, robotics, drones, and autonomous/connected vehicles.

ccs.narrative:
Research on CPS and AV security at CCS began taking shape around 2018, with early work concentrating on CPS security, autonomous vehicles, and industrial control systems. Adversarial Sensor Attack on LiDAR-based Perception in Autonomous Driving (CCS 2019) set an influential baseline by showing how to Demonstrates spoofing LiDAR sensor inputs to inject fake obstacles, fooling autonomous-vehicle perception models. Parallel contributions—Seeing isn't Believing: Towards More Robust Adversarial Attack Against Real World Object Detectors (2019) and Detecting Attacks Against Robotic Vehicles: A Control Invariant Approach (2018) —reinforced the foundational challenges in this space.

A productive wave of CCS work from 2020–2022 deepened the area. Phantom of the ADAS: Securing Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems from Split-Second Phantom Attacks (CCS 2020) advanced the field by demonstrating Demonstrates split-second phantom attacks that fool commercial ADAS into reacting to depthless projected images. Other strong contributions included I Can See the Light: Attacks on Autonomous Vehicles Using Invisible Lights (2021), DriveFuzz: Discovering Autonomous Driving Bugs through Driving Quality-Guided Fuzzing (2022), broadening the space of techniques and targets.

The most recent CCS contributions (from 2023 onward) reflect a maturing field that pushes into harder targets and broader threat models. TileMask: A Passive-Reflection-based Attack against mmWave Radar Object Detection in Autonomous Driving (CCS 2023) exemplified this trend by tackling Passive reflective tiles attack mmWave radar object detection to hide objects from autonomous-driving perception. Similarly, Rust for Embedded Systems: Current State and Open Problems (2024) and Secure and Timely GPU Execution in Cyber-physical Systems (2023) show how the community continues to scale and adapt its methods.

ndss.narrative:
Cyber-physical and autonomous vehicle security at NDSS began with attacks on the cooperative sensing systems that underpin modern traffic and industrial control. Exposing Congestion Attack on Emerging Connected Vehicle based Traffic Signal Control (NDSS 2018) showed how spoofed vehicle data can degrade traffic flow, while A Systematic Framework to Generate Invariants for Anomaly Detection in Industrial Control Systems (NDSS 2019) offered a systematic defense for ICS environments using physical invariants.

The 2020–2022 period saw a rapid escalation in the sophistication of sensor-spoofing attacks. Metamorph (NDSS 2020) demonstrated inaudible adversarial audio that survives over-the-air transmission; Fooling the Eyes of Autonomous Vehicles (NDSS 2022) created robust physical adversarial patches for traffic-sign recognition DNNs; SemperFi (NDSS 2022) countered GPS spoofing for UAVs; and PGFuzz (NDSS 2021) introduced policy-guided fuzzing for robotic vehicle control software, bridging the fuzzing and CPS communities.

Recent work has pushed into even more physically aggressive territory. Paralyzing Drones via EMI Signal Injection (NDSS 2023) and PhantomLiDAR (NDSS 2025) showed that electromagnetic interference can corrupt IMU and LiDAR data at the hardware level, while Invisible Reflections (NDSS 2024) and On the Realism of LiDAR Spoofing Attacks (NDSS 2025) stress-tested sensor manipulation under real-world conditions of speed and distance. The narrative has moved from demonstrating that attacks are possible to quantifying when and how severely they threaten production systems.

uss.narrative:
The earliest USENIX Security work in this area zeroed in on a recurring theme: cyber-physical systems trust their sensors, and that trust is exploitable. "BlackIoT: IoT Botnet of High Wattage Devices Can Disrupt the Power Grid" (USENIX 2018) showed that a botnet of high-wattage appliances could destabilize the power grid by manipulating demand, while "All Your GPS Are Belong To Us: Towards Stealthy Manipulation of Road Navigation Systems" (USENIX 2018) and "Injected and Delivered: Fabricating Implicit Control over Actuation Systems by Spoofing Inertial Sensors" (USENIX 2018) demonstrated that spoofing the physical signals a system depends on (GPS, inertial sensors) could quietly hijack its decisions. The common insight was that the attack surface lives in the physical channel, not just the software.

From 2019 onward the field both broadened across domains and matured toward systematic defense. Vehicle internals and adjacent infrastructure got attention with "CANvas: Fast and Inexpensive Automotive Network Mapping" (USENIX 2019) and "Losing the Car Keys: Wireless PHY-Layer Insecurity in EV Charging" (USENIX 2019), while "RVFuzzer: Finding Input Validation Bugs in Robotic Vehicles through Control-Guided Testing" (USENIX 2019) brought principled fuzzing to robotic-vehicle control software, and "Not Everything is Dark and Gloomy: Power Grid Protections Against IoT Demand Attacks" (USENIX 2019) answered the 2018 grid attack with concrete protections. The 2020 cohort marks the field's pivot to machine-learning perception as the new battleground: "Towards Robust LiDAR-based Perception in Autonomous Driving" (USENIX 2020) proved black-box sensor attacks could fool LiDAR perception, while "SAVIOR: Securing Autonomous Vehicles with Robust Physical Invariants" (USENIX 2020) and "From Control Model to Program: Investigating Robotic Aerial Vehicle Accidents with MAYDAY" (USENIX 2020) pushed physics-based invariants and accident forensics as systematic defenses.

The early 2020s show a clear split between sharper perception attacks and architecture-level defenses. On the attack side, "Too Good to Be Safe: Tricking Lane Detection in Autonomous Driving with Crafted Perturbations" (USENIX 2021), "Rolling Colors: Adversarial Laser Exploits against Traffic Light Recognition" (USENIX 2022), and "TPatch: A Triggered Physical Adversarial Patch" (USENIX 2023) kept finding new ways to deceive vision pipelines, and "An Experimental Study of GPS Spoofing and Takeover Attacks on UAVs" (USENIX 2022) carried the 2018 spoofing thread into real-world drone takeover. On the defense side, "HAWatcher: Semantics-Aware Anomaly Detection for Appified Smart Homes" (USENIX 2021) and "M2MON: Building an MMIO-based Security Reference Monitor for Unmanned Vehicles" (USENIX 2021) built reference monitors and semantics-aware anomaly detection, while fuzzing reached industrial control with "ICSFuzz" (USENIX 2021).

By 2023 the area had widened again to include the human and integrity layers. "That Person Moves Like A Car: Misclassification Attack Detection for Autonomous Systems Using Spatiotemporal Consistency" (USENIX 2023) and "ARI: Attestation of Real-time Mission Execution Integrity" (USENIX 2023) reflect a shift from finding attacks to verifying that perception and mission execution stay trustworthy, and "Exploring User Reactions and Mental Models Towards Perceptual Manipulation Attacks in Mixed Reality" (USENIX 2023) signals the field's expansion into AR/VR and human perception. Across roughly five years the area travelled from "your sensors can be spoofed" to a mature agenda spanning physical-signal attacks, ML-perception robustness, runtime monitoring, and execution-integrity attestation.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this list (2018) splits along two fronts that defined the field's opening moves. One front targets the physical-sensing layer of cyber-physical systems: papers like "Injected and Delivered: Fabricating Implicit Control over Actuation Systems by Spoofing Inertial Sensors" (USENIX 2018) and "All Your GPS Are Belong To Us" (USENIX 2018) showed that attackers could manipulate the analog signals systems trust — inertial sensors, GPS — to seize control of drones and mislead road navigation. The other front is defensive and process-aware: "Detecting Attacks Against Robotic Vehicles: A Control Invariant Approach" (CCS 2018) and "Learning from Mutants" (S&P 2018) introduced the idea that physical control laws and learned invariants can flag when a CPS is being manipulated, while "Scission" (CCS 2018) fingerprinted senders on automotive buses. A third theme arrived via "BlackIoT" (USENIX 2018), which reframed commodity IoT as a weapon against the power grid.

The 2019-2020 period is dominated by a breakthrough that reorients the whole area toward autonomous-vehicle perception. "Adversarial Sensor Attack on LiDAR-based Perception in Autonomous Driving" (CCS 2019) — by far the most cited paper here — demonstrated that spoofed LiDAR points could fool 3D object detection, and "Towards Robust LiDAR-based Perception" (USENIX 2020) followed with a general black-box attack plus countermeasures. Sensor-spoofing matured into a science: "Trick or Heat?" (CCS 2019) and "Hall Spoofing" (USENIX 2020) hit temperature and Hall sensors, and "SoK: A Minimalist Approach to Formalizing Analog Sensor Security" (S&P 2020) finally formalized this growing attack class. Defenses kept pace, moving from ad-hoc detection toward principled physical invariants in "SAVIOR" (USENIX 2020) and "RVFuzzer" (USENIX 2019), which fuzzed robotic-vehicle control software to find input-validation bugs.

By 2021-2023 the perception attacks became more realistic and more complete. "Invisible for both Camera and LiDAR" (S&P 2021) broke multi-sensor fusion — the very design assumed to be robust because it combines modalities — while "Poltergeist" (S&P 2021) and "I Can See the Light" (CCS 2021) attacked cameras through acoustics and invisible light, and "Phantom of the ADAS" (CCS 2020) tricked production driver-assistance systems with split-second projected images. The community also matured methodologically: "DriveFuzz" (CCS 2022) brought systematic fuzzing to whole autonomous-driving stacks, "SoK: Security and Privacy in the Age of Commercial Drones" (S&P 2021) consolidated the drone literature, and "PLA-LiDAR" (S&P 2023) pushed physical laser attacks to richer 3D-detection targets. Across the same span, the smart-home/IoT thread stayed active with "HAWatcher" (USENIX 2021) and "IoTSafe" (NDSS 2021) enforcing safety via discovered physical interactions. The arc, then, runs from isolated single-sensor spoofs to attacks on fused, learning-based perception — met by an increasingly formal toolkit of invariants, attestation, and fuzzing.
